name: Leinong Naga
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wayesha, Ahsi James. 2010. A phonological description of Leinong Naga. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. 186 pp.
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'Suprasegmental phonology: Tone', sec. 3.1 Introduction and 3.2 Tone system, p.47; sec. 6.2 'Suggestions for further study', p.87 p.65 read as an image, both pages also.
catalog_quote: The discussion in this chapter primarily focuses on tone system in Leinong Naga. Each of the four contrastive tones /high, mid, low, stopped/ will be described and demonstrated. This chapter also discusses the distribution of the four tones, two allotones of stopped tone and two processes of tone sandhi in Leinong Naga. Although, there might be stress and intonation in Leinong Naga, they will not be discussed in this chapter, because the data collected in this study was citation forms and not connected speech. ... [3.2 Tone system] ... Leinong Naga is a tonal language like other related Tibeto-Burman languages. It makes use of differences in pitch, which change the core meaning of the word (Burquest 2001: 186). There are two level tones, and two contour tones in Leinong Naga. The two level tones are high stopped (SP), and mid-level (M) tones. The two contour tones are high falling (H), and Low falling (L) tones. Hereafter the four tones will be referred to as H, M, L, and SP respectively. ... [p.87, 6.2 Suggestions for further study] Another issue which needs further research is suprasegmental phonology, for exampleː intonation, stress, and others related to tone.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Leinong Naga is described as a four-tone language (high falling /53/, mid /33/, low falling /21/, stopped /44/ with glottalised allotone on open syllables); every syllable carries tone. The author explicitly declines to analyse stress (data were citation forms only) and flags stress as future work; no placement rule, no claim that stress is absent or non-contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only related structural facts are toned schwa presyllables/prefixes (e.g. nominal prefix /ə⁵³-/, numeral first syllables /bə²¹, sə²¹/) and tone sandhi in compounds and causatives — no prominence claims attached.
new_statements.domain_note: Data are a 1,500-item elicited wordlist in citation form from Lahe town speakers; the deferral of stress is explicitly because no connected speech was collected.
new_statements.identity_note: Wayesha 2010 describes Leinong Naga as spoken in and around Lahe town, Lahe township, Naga Self-Administered Zone (Sagaing), Myanmar = Glottolog lein1237 'Lainong Naga' (ISO lzn); 'Leinong' and 'Lainong' are spelling variants of the same variety (van Dam 2026). van Dam 2018 notes possible overlap of Lainong with Htangan and Nahen varieties but Wayesha's data are Lahe-town Leinong proper.

tone_statements.quote: Lainong, however, is a Southeastern variety which also falls within Stage I. Lainong also underwent loss of codas on CVʔ syllables, but this did not result in a tone change. Instead, there are group A reflexes with a 53: contour, B with 33: contour, and C with 21:. All reflexes of group D stems have a 44: contour, regardless of whether they are CVC or CV syllables.

tone_statements.summary: Comparative tonogenesis paper: Lainong reflexes of the four proto categories are A 53, B 33, C 21, D 44 (Chao values), data from Wayesha 2010; count taken from this closed list, no stated total.

sources.note: Ch.3 'Suprasegmental phonology: Tone' (p.47): Leinong Naga is tonal with four contrastive tones (high falling 53, mid 33, low falling 21, stopped 44) plus tone sandhi; stress and intonation are explicitly NOT analysed ('there might be stress and intonation.. they will not be discussed.. because the data collected in this study was citation forms'); p.87 lists 'intonation, stress' as topics needing further research. No statement of stress placement anywhere in the thesis.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2018. The tone system of Tangsa-Nocte and related Northern Naga varieties. PhD thesis, La Trobe University. Appendix C 'Lainong', pp.301-305.
sources.note: Appendix C gives Lainong tonemes (low falling, high with fall, mid; checked syllables as a fourth category per consultant Anui Sainyiu) with Praat pitch tracks from Morey's 2014 recordings; body text (p.66, ch.5) says Lainong's tone system is clearly distinct from Tangsa-Nocte. No mention of stress/accent for Lainong.

sources.citation: Sainyiu, Anui. 2026. The Living Song of Kaīvi: Lainong Oral Tradition and Cultural Resilience in Northwestern Myanmar. Himalayan Linguistics 25(2): 114-135. doi:10.5070/H9.68590
sources.note: Anthropological-linguistic study of the Kaīvi and Kaīvi Yuīnyiū song genres 'composed in an archaic register of the Lainong language' (Crossref abstract); no tone content is stated in the abstract. As a Himalayan Linguistics article by a trained native-speaker linguist it plausibly carries a short language-background section (phoneme and four-tone inventory, tone-marking orthography with macron/grave diacritics as in Kaīvi, Zëūdiāng-Lainòng) and tone-marked song texts, which would be the first published Lainong text material; this is an inference from genre, not seen.
